This guide answers the running question in one short script:

> Among people admitted with appendicitis, how many are readmitted within 30
> days of discharge, and is that more common in people with diabetes?

The script repeats the earlier guides' steps, so its numbers match theirs.
If you have done those guides, here are all their steps together. If you start
here, read for the shape of the analysis, and use the links to go back to the
guide behind any step:

1. Connect to the database: [Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html).
2. Stack the yearly tables and convert their dates with `thip_table()`:
   [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html#stack-the-tables-convert-the-dates).
3. Audit the dates with `thip_date_audit()`:
   [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html#audit-the-dates-before-you-filter).
4. Select the candidate records on the database with `thip_filter_icd()`:
   [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html#select-the-candidate-records).
5. Choose one entry per person in R:
   [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html#choose-one-entry-per-person).
6. Fetch the follow-up with `thip_window()` and mark readmissions:
   [Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html#plan-the-follow-up).
7. Fetch the look-back history:
   [Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html#look-back-a-year).
8. Flag diabetes with `icd_flag()`: [Flag conditions](condition-flags.html).
9. Summarise readmission by diabetes: this page.

As in every guide, the code runs on the example database that comes with
thipR. On THIP, connect with `thip_connect()` instead, after the one-time setup
in [Start here](start-here.html), and the same code runs there, apart from the
differences in [The example is DuckDB, THIP is
ClickHouse](database-from-r.html#the-example-is-duckdb-thip-is-clickhouse).

## Connect, stack and audit

Load the packages, connect, stack the three yearly tables with their dates
converted, and audit the dates:

```{r stack}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

# 1. Connect (on THIP: con <- thip_connect())
con <- thip_connect_example()

# 2. Stack the yearly tables and convert the dates
admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d")
)

# 3. Audit the dates
date_audit <- thip_date_audit(
  admissions,
  columns = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc")
)
knitr::kable(date_audit)
```

Every admission date was read;
`r date_audit$n_failed[date_audit$field == "dsc"]` discharge dates failed and
`r date_audit$n_blank[date_audit$field == "dsc"]` is blank. Step 5 keeps only
candidates with a discharge date, so none of these records can become an entry.

## Candidates and entries

Select the study period's appendicitis admissions on the database, bring them
into R, and keep each person's first one with a discharge date:

```{r entries}
# 4. Select candidates on the database and collect them
candidates <- admissions |>
  filter(adm >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
         adm <= as.Date("2024-08-31")) |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "K35", cols = "pdx",
                  match = "prefix") |>
  collect()

# 5. One entry per person: the first with a discharge date
entries <- candidates |>
  filter(!is.na(dsc)) |>
  arrange(pid, adm, tran_id) |>
  distinct(pid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(pid, entry_id = tran_id,
         adm_date = adm, dsc_date = dsc)

c(entries = nrow(entries), people = n_distinct(entries$pid))
```

That gives `r nrow(entries)` entries from `r n_distinct(entries$pid)` people,
each with an `entry_id`, an admission date and a discharge date.

## Follow up and look back

Fetch each entry's admissions on days 1 to 30 after discharge and in the 365
days before admission, and mark the entries that were readmitted:

```{r windows}
# 6. Follow-up: admissions on days 1 to 30 after discharge
followup <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx) |>
  thip_window(entries, date = "adm", index = "dsc_date",
              window = c(1L, 31L)) |>
  collect()

readmit <- entries |>
  left_join(
    count(followup, entry_id, name = "readmissions"),
    by = "entry_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(readmissions = coalesce(readmissions, 0L),
         readmitted = readmissions > 0)

count(readmit, readmitted)

# 7. Look-back: admissions in the 365 days before admission
history <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx,
         num_range("sdx", 1:20)) |>
  thip_window(entries, date = "adm", index = "adm_date",
              window = c(-365L, 0L)) |>
  collect()
```

`r sum(readmit$readmitted)` of the `r nrow(readmit)` entries were readmitted
within 30 days; `readmit` starts from `entries`, so it keeps the other
`r sum(!readmit$readmitted)` too. `history` leaves out the entry admission
itself, so step 8 takes that admission's codes from `candidates`.

## Flag diabetes

Flag each entry whose own admission, or an admission in its `history`, has a
code starting with E10 to E14 in any diagnosis column (`match = "prefix"`):

```{r flags}
# 8. Flag diabetes on the entry admission and its history
entry_admissions <- candidates |>
  filter(tran_id %in% entries$entry_id) |>
  rename(entry_id = tran_id)

flags <- bind_rows(entry_admissions, history) |>
  icd_flag(
    conditions = list(diabetes = paste0("E", 10:14)),
    id = "entry_id",
    cols = c("pdx", paste0("sdx", 1:20)),
    match = "prefix"
  ) |>
  mutate(diabetes = coalesce(diabetes, FALSE))

count(flags, diabetes)
```

[Flag conditions](condition-flags.html) flags the two periods separately to show
what looking back adds, then checks that this one call gives the same answer;
`coalesce()` reads `NA` (no codes recorded) as `FALSE` (no diabetes code
recorded), as that guide does.

Of the `r nrow(flags)` entries, `r sum(flags$diabetes)` have a diabetes code.
The flag looks only at the entry admission and the year before it, never at
the follow-up, and `FALSE` means no code was recorded there, not that the
person has no diabetes.

## Readmission by diabetes

Join the flags onto `readmit`, keeping every entry, and count readmissions with
and without diabetes:

```{r summary}
# 9. Summarise readmission by diabetes, keeping every entry
results <- readmit |>
  left_join(flags, by = "entry_id")

summary_table <- results |>
  group_by(diabetes) |>
  summarise(entries = n(), readmitted = sum(readmitted)) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * readmitted / entries, 1))

knitr::kable(summary_table)
```

The two rows add up to all `r sum(summary_table$entries)` entries. In the
example, readmission is more common with diabetes:
`r summary_table$percent[summary_table$diabetes]`% against
`r summary_table$percent[!summary_table$diabetes]`% without.

## What leaves THIP

The summary table is the only thing you take out of THIP, and first it must
pass your project's rule for small counts. With `min_count <- 10`, as in [Using
THIP data responsibly](responsible-use.html#small-counts), both readmitted
counts, `r summary_table$readmitted[1]` and `r summary_table$readmitted[2]`,
would be hidden, and so would their percentages, which give the counts back.
Hide them, then write the table to a file; here a temporary one:

```{r export}
min_count <- 10  # set this from your protocol

shared <- summary_table |>
  mutate(
    percent = if_else(readmitted < min_count,
                      NA_real_, percent),
    readmitted = if_else(readmitted < min_count,
                         paste0("<", min_count),
                         as.character(readmitted))
  )

summary_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(shared, summary_file, row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(readLines(summary_file))
```

The file holds counts for two groups and nothing about any one person; the
hidden percentages read `NA`. Everything else stays in your R session, which on
THIP runs inside your THIP account: the records that came in at the three
`collect()`s (`candidates`, `followup` and `history`) and the tables made from
them.

## What a real study adds

The example's records are invented ([Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html)),
so its numbers say nothing about real readmission rates. A study built on this
script adds:

- **A protocol fixed in advance:** the question, study period, code lists,
  windows and analysis, written down before you run the script on THIP. The
  example database lets you write and test every step first.
- **Reviewed code lists:** K35 and E10 to E14 illustrate the method and are not
  validated definitions. Use lists reviewed for your question, and look at
  which codes occur in your records.
- **Eligibility rules**, such as a minimum age added to the `filter()` in step 4
  ([From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html#other-eligibility-rules)),
  or leaving out entry admissions that ended in death, since those people
  cannot be readmitted.
- **Confidence intervals and adjustment:** an interval for each percentage, for
  example from `binom.test()`, and a model that adjusts for age and sex, such
  as logistic regression with `glm(..., family = binomial)`, after keeping
  `age_y` and `sex` in step 5's `select()` and converting `age_y` with
  `as.integer()`.
- **Readmissions counted once per entry:** the table counts entries readmitted
  at least once, not readmission records. To report how many readmissions there
  were, first check that no record came back twice for an entry, as in
  [Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html#count-readmissions-per-entry).
- **Checks on the data first**, from [Check before you trust](data-checks.html).
  One matters here already: part of the look-back year of the
  `r sum(entries$adm_date < as.Date("2022-10-01"))` entries admitted in fiscal
  year 2565 falls before the first table you stacked, so it was never searched
  ([Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html#windows-and-the-years-you-stacked)
  gives two fixes).

Next: [Check before you trust](data-checks.html), the checks to run on the data
before you rely on a result like this one.

```{r disconnect, include = FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```
